name: The Federal Government Wants You To Know It Still Exists
author: the Gray Zone Dispatch, unsigned editorial
description: A satirical piece from a GLMZ zine about the Federal Remnant government in Denver — funny until it isn't.
body:
Great news. The Federal Government of the United States of America wants you to know that it is still there. It is in Denver. It has been in Denver since 2119, when the forty-ninth iteration of emergency relocation protocols placed the continuity government in the Rocky Mountain Resilience Complex, which is a bunker, which is where the federal government has been for the better part of a century, in a bunker, in Denver, being the government.

The Federal Remnant — which it insists we not call the Federal Remnant — has issued a press release asking media outlets to use its official designation, which is 'The Continuing Federal Government of the United States.' It issued this press release in 2209. We are running it now because we only received it last week, which tells you something about their communications infrastructure.

The CFG (we are using the initialism to save space) has a President, a Congress of forty-three members representing territories that are geographically distributed across a nation that mostly does not recognize their jurisdiction, and a Supreme Court of four justices. The fifth seat has been vacant since Justice Petrov-Asante retired in 2207. The CFG has been unable to confirm a replacement because the confirmation process requires Senate approval and the Senate meets twice a year in Denver for sessions that last between two and four days. The Senate has a lot on its plate. The fifth seat remains vacant.

What does the CFG actually do? We are glad you asked, because the answer is 'more than you think' and we find this information both amusing and vaguely unsettling, which seems about right.

The CFG controls the GPS satellite network. All of it. This is a fact that most GLMZ residents do not know and would find surprising if they did. The Global Positioning System was a US Department of Defense asset before the Consolidation, and in the chaos of the Consolidation period, the CFG's predecessor continuity government retained control of the satellite array through a combination of technical access and the fact that nobody else bothered to take it. The satellites still work. The network still broadcasts. Every navigation system in GLMZ, every freight routing algorithm, every BCI location service uses GPS signals that are, technically, operated by the same government that has been in a bunker in Denver for ninety years. They could turn it off. They have mentioned this, twice, in diplomatic communications to the corponation consortium. The corponations paid the annual maintenance fee both times.

The CFG also still issues passports. About fourteen thousand people per year apply for them. This is not because those fourteen thousand people believe in the CFG or recognize its sovereignty. It is because a US passport, even one issued by a skeleton government in a Denver bunker, is still legally recognized in several Pacific Rim jurisdictions and three African Union territories where GLMZ transit documents are not. The passport photographs look normal. The seal is correct. The document numbers are sequential. Bureaucracy is the most durable form of government.

The current President is Esperanza Volkov-Nakamura, age sixty-seven, fourth-term, previously the Secretary of Transportation for the CFG, elevated to the presidency after the previous President retired for health reasons. She holds press conferences that are attended by seven journalists, three of whom represent foreign governments with reasons to maintain the legal fiction of US continuity. She is, by all accounts, a serious person doing an absurd job with complete sincerity, and it is hard not to respect that, in the way it is hard not to respect the person who keeps showing up to fix the elevator in a building that is mostly rubble.

We are including, without comment, that the CFG recently passed legislation — through its forty-three-member Congress, in a Denver bunker — designating GLMZ as a 'Federal Special Economic Zone' and specifying that GLMZ residents are entitled to representation in Congress. The GLMZ Municipal Authority's response was a one-sentence acknowledgment that they had received the notification. The Gradient Compact's response was silence. The corponation consortium's response was a letter that our legal correspondent describes as 'extremely polite laughter.'

The GPS satellites keep working. The passports keep being issued. The federal government of the United States, in its bunker in Denver, keeps being the federal government of the United States, and somewhere in there is a joke we haven't quite finished laughing at yet.
